attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. The Wierda quote that follows is separate and not part of this claim.

semantics.note: Faithfully records three present-tense observations: large losses, efforts to raise prices, and customer resistance, with the named providers given as examples.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: net loss for Q1 2026, and pricing and customer reactions through the post date. Treating the named providers as examples, not a requirement for every provider, is fair to the speaker. No accounting basis is supplied, so the money element depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Dated May 2026 report of Anthropic changes that raised effective costs, with attributable user backlash. It covers pricing and resistance for Anthropic only, not losses.

Press account, published before the cutoff, of OpenAI's Q1 2026 net loss as given in shareholder documents. It is an estimate on an unstated basis and covers one provider, so it does not settle the comparable-loss component.

reviews.rationale: The pricing and customer-resistance parts hold for Anthropic (e1). The losses part rests on a single press estimate for OpenAI, with no comparable records for Anthropic or Cursor. Nothing contradicts the claim, but the packet does not meet the support condition for losses among the named providers.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'And so on' adds no specific institutions.

contract.note: Reading 'inundating' as a substantial, recurring influx that creates a review burden is ordinary. Counting submissions and workload is fair to the speaker. Whether supplier screening counts as 'libraries' is a matter of interpretation.

evidence.note: Wikipedia RfC closure dated May 2026 cites increasing improper AI use and a cleanup backlog. This supports the Wikipedia part.

Disclosure by Hoopla, a library supplier: about 20,000 titles declined in January 2026, mixing AI-generated and low-quality titles, which it says never reached libraries. It shows heavy screening without proving the problem is negligible or what actually reached libraries.

reviews.rationale: The Wikipedia part is supported by a dated moderation record. For libraries there is only a supplier's self-report that mixes AI and low-quality titles and says they were screened out. That neither establishes nor refutes an influx burdening libraries. The support condition needs both institutions, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. The Washington Post graph he goes on to cite is separate material.

semantics.note: The firm part is causal: GenAI led to more books. The quality and sales clauses are hedged ('not clear') and are correctly kept as qualifiers rather than claims.

contract.note: Scoring only the firm supply claim, and checking that the hedged clauses are not contradicted, is fair to the speaker. Reading quality as average quality is ordinary. Amazon e-books stand in for books in general, which is an interpretive choice.

evidence.note: NBER summary from May 2026, before the post: Amazon e-book releases nearly tripled after LLMs arrived, a rise the authors attribute to LLM availability, and average quality fell. Gains at absolute rank positions and in welfare do not show better average books or higher sales.

reviews.rationale: Research available before the post links LLMs to a near-tripling of e-book releases and finds lower average quality. The hedged doubts about quality and sales are not contradicted. One limit: the evidence covers the Amazon e-book segment and does not fully isolate AI's causal role.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Reading 'especially in agentic coding' as an emphasis within wider AI losses is faithful to the text. The 'food chain' scope is preserved.

contract.note: Reading the claim as large realized losses across several business layers in Q1 2026 is ordinary. Asking for evidence of the coding emphasis follows from 'especially'. No accounting basis is supplied.

evidence.note: Anthropic S-1, filed before the cutoff: Q1 2026 GAAP net loss of about $14.4B, mostly a fair-value charge, and an operating loss of about $1.7B. The figures are company-wide with no coding allocation, and adjusted net income for H1 2026 was positive.
CoreWeave's own Q1 2026 disclosure: GAAP net loss of $740M. This shows losses at the infrastructure layer but says nothing about coding.
Secondary report that Cursor lost about $900M in its last fiscal year, with negative gross margins. Wrong period and unspecified loss measure.

reviews.rationale: Losses appear at several layers, but the measures and periods are not comparable. Anthropic's GAAP loss is mostly a valuation charge, and the Cursor figure covers a different period. No evidence ties the losses specifically to agentic coding, which the contract requires. Nothing contradicts the claim, but the packet does not meet the support condition.
